title: Bike recalls, read like surveillance data. Which parts fail, which hazards follow, and what is changing.
text:
What this is
Recalls are a regulator’s response to a safety problem, so a collection of them can be read the way an epidemiologist reads disease notifications. This project applies that approach to bicycles:

A case definition. Written rules decide which recalls count (bicycles, e-bikes, components, and accessories) and which do not (helmets, exercise bikes, scooters, and motorbikes), with every decision recorded.
Classification. Each recall is coded by what was recalled, the part that failed, and the hazard it caused.
Validation. The rules were checked against 100 hand-labelled records, with a further 40 held back as an independent test.
Caveats. Recalls are passively reported and negotiated, and regulations have changed over time. Those limits shape what these numbers can and cannot say.

The analysis is industry-wide. It does not rank or compare companies. Brand names appear only in the searchable table, as they appear in the official notices.

title: Bike recalls, read like surveillance data. Which parts fail, which hazards follow, and what is changing.
text:
Key findings



Falls dominate


91% of recall events involve a fall or crash hazard. Fire, laceration, and chemical hazards together make up the rest.




Forks fail most often


22% of events trace back to the fork, ahead of stems and handlebars, wheels and hubs, and frames.




E-bike recalls are rising


There were 18 e-bike recall events in 2023 to 2025, against 9 in the three years before. Some of that may reflect growth in e-bike sales, which these data cannot measure.




E-bikes bring fire


25% of e-bike recall events involve a fire or burn hazard, against 2% of other bicycle recalls, mostly from batteries and chargers.




Recalls are not injuries. A recall shows that a regulator and a company acted on a problem, not how many people were hurt. There is no count of bikes sold, so these figures cannot be read as risk. More pages, including the full surveillance caveats, are on the way.

Matching recalls

listRows = filtered
  .map(d => ({
    year: d.recall_year,
    country: eventCountries.get(d.event_id).size > 1 ? "Both" : (d.country === "United States" ? "US" : "Canada"),
    title: d.title,
    url: d.url,
    what: d.product_form,
    part: d.failed_component,
    hazard: d.hazard_group,
    status: d.case_status
  }))
  .sort((a, b) => b.year - a.year)







viewof search = Inputs.search(listRows, {placeholder: "Search titles, parts, hazards...", label: "Search"})







Inputs.table(search, {
  columns: ["year", "country", "title", "what", "part", "hazard"],
  header: {year: "Year", country: "Country", title: "Recall notice", what: "What was recalled", part: "Failed part", hazard: "Hazard"},
  format: {title: (t, i, rows) => html`<a href=${rows[i].url} target="_blank" rel="noopener">${t}</a>`},
  width: {year: 60, country: 80, title: 420},
  rows: 12,
  layout: "auto"
})







html`<p class="dash-note">Titles link to the official notice. Brand names appear only as published by the regulator. For joint recalls, the US notice is shown.</p>`







DOM.download(() => new Blob([d3.csvFormat(listRows)], {type: "text/csv"}), "bike_recalls_filtered.csv", `Download these ${fmtN(listRows.length)} recalls (CSV)`)
